newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine oil buffer fund down to 771 mln pesos.
newsitem.headline: Philippine oil buffer fund down to 771 mln pesos.

text.p: The Department of Energy (DOE) said on Tuesday the one billion pesos infused into the Oil Price Stabilisation Fund (OPSF) had dwindled to 771.7 million pesos as of end September 1996.

Energy Undersecretary Benhur Salcedo said in the latest OPSF report that reduction was a result of a withdrawal of an average of 8.20 centavos per litre of petroleum product from the one billion fund due to the 6.95 centavo average per litre increase last Sept 13.
Salcedo said the fund is estimated to decrease further to 656.5 million pesos due to the 30.72 centavo average per litre increase in October.

The one billion buffer fund was contributed by the Philippine National Oil Co to the OPSF to absorb increases in excess of 50 centavos per litre of petroleum products since government implemented an automatic oil price formula in August as a prelude to full oil industry deregulation in March 1997.

The one billion peso fund was meant to iron out price fluctuations after August. The deficit incurred by the OPSF before that still remains. As of end September, the OPSF deficit stood at 2.376 billion pesos from 2.331 billion in August.

The energy official said that based on the latest OPSF report, Petron Corp still has the biggest claims of 1.085 billion pesos, followed by Pilipinas Shell Petroleum Corp, a unit of the Royal Dutch/Shell Group at 928.09 million pesos.
Caltex Philippines Inc, a joint venture between Chevron Corp and Texaco Inc, is entitled to a 388.35 million peso claims.

The OPSF is a buffer fund which cushions domestic pump prices from fluctuations in crude cost and the foreign exchange rate. When crude prices are high and the peso weakens against the dollar, the oil firms are allowed to withdraw from the fund. Oil firms are required to contribute to the fund when the reverse happens.
Under the deregulation law, the fund will be abolished once the oil industry is fully deregulated.
